lesson.title: Drawing the Path Your Program Takes
lesson.summary: Flowcharts represent an algorithm's logic visually, using shapes and arrows to trace the exact path a program takes through decisions and actions.
lesson.body:
Pseudocode describes an algorithm in words. A flowchart describes the same kind of logic in pictures. Both are tools for algorithm design, and many programmers sketch a flowchart first when an algorithm has several branching paths, since a diagram can make the possible routes through the logic easier to see at a glance than a block of text.

Flowcharts use a small set of standard shapes. An oval marks the start or end of the algorithm. A rectangle represents a step or action, such as assigning a value to a variable. A diamond represents a decision point, where the flow splits based on a yes or no question. A parallelogram represents input or output, such as reading a value or displaying a result. Arrows connect these shapes and show the direction the algorithm flows, including the loops that send the flow backward to repeat a step.

Take the simple problem of deciding whether a number is even or odd. As a flowchart, the logic looks like this:

Start
  -> Input n
  -> Decision: is n % 2 == 0 ?
       -> Yes -> Output "even" -> End
       -> No  -> Output "odd" -> End

Every path through this diagram ends at the same End oval, but which path is taken depends entirely on the answer at the diamond. This is exactly the kind of branching that is awkward to describe in a single sentence but immediate to see in a picture: one input, one decision, two possible outputs.

Once the flowchart is settled, translating it into code is direct, because each shape maps onto a familiar programming construct. Ovals become the start and end of a function, rectangles become statements, parallelograms become input and output calls, and diamonds become if statements:

def even_or_odd(n):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return "even"
    else:
        return "odd"

print(even_or_odd(7))
print(even_or_odd(10))

Trace it by hand: for n = 7, the diamond asks whether 7 % 2 == 0. Since 7 % 2 is 1, the answer is no, so the flow takes the "No" arrow and outputs "odd". For n = 10, 10 % 2 is 0, so the answer is yes, the flow takes the "Yes" arrow, and outputs "even". Both runs match what the function prints.

Flowcharts and pseudocode are two views of the same underlying algorithm design, and neither replaces the other. A flowchart is especially good at showing the overall shape of an algorithm, including how many different paths exist and where loops send you back to repeat earlier steps, while pseudocode is often better for spelling out precise details inside a single step. Many algorithm designers move back and forth between the two: sketching a flowchart to nail down the branching structure, then writing pseudocode (or code) to fill in the exact logic inside each box.
